questions.prompt: What does a search engine show you when you search?
options: A brand-new answer written just for you, word by word
Pages that already exist, found in its index and ranked by how relevant they are
Only pages that a person has checked are true
Whatever it remembers from the day it was built
questions.explanation: A search engine crawls the web, stores pages in its index and, when you search, shows the most relevant existing pages with links. It finds; it doesn't write, and it doesn't check whether pages are true.

questions.prompt: Without web search, where does an LLM's answer come from?
options: It copies the top result from a search engine
It phones an expert and types up what they say
It looks the answer up in a database of checked facts
It writes new text, one token at a time, from patterns it learned in training
questions.explanation: On its own, an LLM doesn't look anything up. It predicts what's likely to come next, using what it learned during training, and it doesn't keep track of where each fact came from.

questions.prompt: What is a model's knowledge cutoff?
options: The date its training text stops, after which it knows nothing new on its own
The most words it can write in one answer
The topics it isn't allowed to talk about
The time of day after which it stops answering
questions.explanation: Training text is collected up to a certain date. Meta's Llama 3.1, for example, has a cutoff of December 2023 but was released in July 2024, so it was already months behind on launch day.

questions.prompt: The IPL final was last week. A chatbot with web search switched off confidently names the winner. What should you think?
options: It must be right, because it sounds so sure
It's probably right, because chatbots are updated every day
It can't know about last week from training alone, so check a news site
It's definitely wrong, because chatbots never know anything about cricket
questions.explanation: Anything after the model's knowledge cutoff isn't in its training. Without search, it can only guess, perhaps naming an earlier season's winner, and it sounds just as confident when it's guessing.

questions.prompt: What is a hallucination in an LLM?
options: When the model refuses to answer a question
A plausible-sounding but false statement, such as a made-up fact, quote or reference
When the model answers in the wrong language
A picture the model draws by mistake
questions.explanation: OpenAI's researchers define hallucinations as "plausible but false statements generated by language models". Fake citations, quotes, dates and links are common examples.

questions.prompt: Your friend's project report lists five references that a chatbot suggested. What should she do before she submits it?
options: Nothing, because chatbots only suggest real papers
Ask the chatbot whether the references are real
Delete the references so nobody can check them
Open every reference to check it exists and says what the report claims
questions.explanation: LLMs can invent papers, authors and links that look completely real. Asking the same chatbot doesn't prove anything. The only check is opening each source yourself.

questions.prompt: You need the last date to apply for this year's JEE Main. What's the most reliable way to find it?
options: Search for the official exam website and read the notice there
Ask a chatbot with web search switched off
Use whatever date a friend remembers from last year
Ask a chatbot to guess, then pick the most common answer
questions.explanation: Dates like this change every year, so a model's memory may be out of date. The official notice is the final word, and a search engine is the quickest way to find it.

questions.prompt: Why might an LLM give a confident wrong answer instead of saying "I don't know"?
options: It knows the answer is wrong but wants to please you
Its internet connection dropped halfway through
It writes what's likely to come next, and training has often rewarded guessing over admitting uncertainty
Someone at the company typed the wrong answer in
questions.explanation: A confident guess often looks more like a typical answer than "I don't know". OpenAI's research says training and testing have rewarded guessing, like a test with no negative marking.
